# Optimal contributions and the $\alpha$ constraint {#sec-ocs}

```{r}
#| label: setup-ocs
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
ctx <- simulate_data(book_cfg)
n_sel <- 60
```

@sec-choosing-recommendation recommends putting $\theta$ (computed on lines) and
$N_{e,\text{par}}$ into the optimiser and keeping the expensive metrics for
validation. This chapter states the optimisation problem that recommendation
defines, places it in the optimal-contribution selection (OCS) literature, and says what its
continuous relaxation does and does not bound. $\alpha$ is the relative loss of gene diversity
of @eq-catalogue-alpha (defined in @sec-baseline),

$$\alpha(S) \;=\; \frac{GD_{\text{ref}} - GD_S}{GD_{\text{ref}}}, \qquad
  GD_S = 1 - \theta_S, \qquad
  \theta_S = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i, j \in S} f_{ij},$$ {#eq-ocs-alpha}

with $S$ a set of $n$ hybrids, $f_{ij}$ the molecular coancestry of hybrids $i$
and $j$, $\theta_S = \mathbf{c}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{c}$ for the contribution vector
$c_i = 1/n$ on $S$ (`theta_group()`), and $GD_{\text{ref}}$ the mean $GD$ of
random subsets of size $n$ (`gd_ref`, from `null_distribution()`). The
multi-trait index $u_i$ is `ctx$index`, the known-marker-effects index of
@sec-simulating-crosses; @sec-genomic-prediction shows how a real programme
obtains a `traits` matrix to hand to `stage1_build()` and what accuracy to expect.

## What this chapter assumes

Each item is a restriction on every number below, not a remark.

1. **Inbred parent lines** (A2 of @sec-era-programme). Then $\mathbf{f}$ over hybrids
   is a function of the line matrix $\mathbf{f}^L$ (@sec-collapse).
2. **No dominance, an additive index** (A7 of @sec-era-programme). $\theta$, $GD$ and $\alpha$ are
   functions of allele frequencies alone, and $u_i$ is additive.
3. **The index is the truth.** Every value of $\bar u_S$ below is computed on
   `ctx$index`, not on a prediction. For an exact optimiser, the true index of the
   plan it finds on the truth is at least the true index of the plan it finds on
   predictions, so the values here are an upper limit on what selection on predicted
   values delivers (@sec-choosing-error); the plans of this chapter come from
   heuristics, and the statement is not extended to them.
4. **The marker panel is the causal set** (A5 of @sec-era-programme), in every
   section except the panel sensitivity, where only $\mathbf{f}$ follows the panel
   and the index does not (stated there).
5. **The constraint pins one lens.** $\theta$, $GD$ and $\alpha$ are the
   homozygosity lens; $F_{\text{drift}}$, the lens anchored on the frozen frequencies
   `ctx$p0`, is not pinned by $\alpha$ (@sec-genomic-era). With inbred parents
   $\alpha$ acts on the total $GD_T$, which contains the between-pool term $GD_{BS}$
   that a hybrid programme wants preserved, so a budget on $\alpha$ does not
   isolate the within-pool loss (@sec-response-genic).
6. **Scale.** The teaching scale (A8 of @sec-era-programme): 25 + 25 lines, 2000 markers,
   $N =$ `r ctx$N` hybrids, $n =$ `r n_sel`, simulation seed 1, one founder draw,
   except where a sentence says otherwise.

## Constraint, not a weighted sum

With $\mathbf{u}$ the multi-trait index and $S$ the selected set of size $n$ (`n_sel`):

$$\max_{S,\; |S| = n} \; \bar u_S = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in S} u_i
  \qquad \text{subject to} \qquad \alpha(S) \le \alpha_{\max},$$ {#eq-ocs-problem}

where $\alpha_{\max} \in (0, 1)$ is the **budget**: the loss of gene diversity the
programme accepts. Because $\alpha(S) \le \alpha_{\max}$ is the same as
$\theta_S \le \theta_{\max}$ with

$$\theta_{\max} = 1 - GD_{\text{ref}}\,(1 - \alpha_{\max}),$$ {#eq-ocs-theta-max}

the constraint is a bound on a quadratic form of the contributions.

The common alternative, $\max\; \bar u_S - \lambda\,\theta_S$ with $\lambda \ge 0$,
requires calibrating $\lambda$, which has no direct interpretation. The
constraint form has an operational meaning: *"I accept losing at most
$\alpha_{\max}$ of diversity."* That is a sentence a breeding committee can
approve or reject; "diversity is worth $\lambda = 3.7$ index units" is not.

The two are not equivalent for a discrete problem. The optima of the weighted sum
over all $\lambda$ lie on the upper concave envelope of the set of pairs
$(\theta_S, \bar u_S)$, so a budget that falls between two vertices of that
envelope is the optimum of no $\lambda$. The multiplier is not eliminated by the
constraint form; it is moved from an input to an output: the budget implies one,
and @sec-relaxation reports it. The committee decides the budget;
what the budget costs in index is the analyst's to trace (@fig-ocs-frontier), and
the exchange rate is read off that trace rather than chosen.

The optimiser's fitness is printed below. `decode()` (`R/03_de_select.R`,
@sec-combinatorial) maps the $n$ continuous keys of the differential-evolution
(DE) vector to $n$ distinct hybrids.

```{r}
#| label: ocs-make-fitness
make_fitness
```

The budget violation is
`viol = max(0, alpha - alpha_max)`, the **absolute** excess in units of
$\alpha$, and the fitness subtracts `penalty * viol` with `penalty = 1000` from
$\bar u_S$. The price per unit of $\alpha$ is the same at every budget, so the
price of an overshoot *relative* to the budget is not: a 10% overshoot costs
$1000 \times 0.1 \times \alpha_{\max}$ index units (@tbl-ocs-penalty). The optional `max_use` term adds, in
the same fitness, the number of parent slots used beyond the cap divided by
$2n$, where `max_use` is the largest number of the $n$ selected hybrids that may
share one line as a parent (a count; defined and enforced in
@sec-combinatorial). It defaults to `NULL`, no cap, and is off in this chapter.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ocs-penalty
#| tbl-cap: "Price of a 10% overshoot of the budget in `make_fitness()`, in index units (s.d.). columns: the budget $\\alpha_{\\max}$; overshoot, $0.1\\,\\alpha_{\\max}$, an absolute excess of $\\alpha$; price, $1000 \\times$ overshoot. Teaching scale; the chunk first checks `penalty * viol` against `make_fitness()` itself on the truncation plan, at a binding (1%) and an inactive (5%) budget."
tr <- sel_truncation(ctx, n_sel)
null <- null_distribution(ctx, n_sel, B = 400, B_full = 60)   # seed 7 inside
a_tr <- alpha_loss(tr, ctx, null$gd_ref)
fit  <- function(a) make_fitness(ctx, n_sel, a, null$gd_ref)(tr + 0.5)
pen  <- vapply(c(0.01, 0.05), function(a) fit(a) + mean_index(tr, ctx), numeric(1))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(pen, 1000 * pmax(0, a_tr - c(0.01, 0.05)))))   # 5% is inactive
ov <- 0.1 * c(0.01, 0.05)
knitr::kable(fmt(data.frame(alpha_max = c(0.01, 0.05), overshoot = ov, price = 1000 * ov), 4),
             col.names = c("$\\alpha_{\\max}$", "overshoot", "price (index s.d.)"))
```

So the constraint is enforced by a linear penalty, not refused at any price: a DE
plan can end with a small violation, and `alpha_loss()` of the returned plan must
be checked. The bound of @eq-ocs-bound treats the budget as exact.

### The constrained form is older than this book

@kempthorne1959 pose, for selection indices, the problem of maximising progress
in an aggregate genotype subject to no expected change in specified linear
functions of the genetic values (the problem statement was read in the full text
by the reference check of this chapter; their solution was not read for this
book). @sec-response gives the matrix form of that restricted index as the
book's own statement, not claimed to be theirs, and lists four differences that
keep it from being the $\alpha$ constraint (equality against inequality,
expectation against realisation, a trait against $GD_T$, closed form against
search). The one numerical fact used here is that the restricted index holds its
restricted direction at zero to rounding, on the two-trait example of
@tbl-response-restricted, with $\boldsymbol\Sigma_P$ the phenotypic and
$\boldsymbol\Sigma_G$ the genetic covariance matrix of the traits (`P` and `Sg`
in the code), $\mathbf{a}$ the economic weights and $\mathbf{R}$ the restricted
direction (moisture):

```{r}
#| label: ocs-restricted-zero
P  <- matrix(c(4.0, 1.2, 1.2, 1.0), 2)      # Sigma_P, as in 02b
Sg <- matrix(c(2.0, 0.3, 0.3, 0.3), 2)      # Sigma_G, as in 02b
a  <- c(1, 1); R <- cbind(c(0, 1))
stopifnot(all(eigen(Sg, only.values = TRUE)$values > 0),     # a covariance
          all(eigen(P - Sg, only.values = TRUE)$values > 0))
cov_R <- c(unrestricted = drop(crossprod(R, Sg %*% index_smith_hazel(P, Sg, a))),
           restricted   = drop(crossprod(R, Sg %*% index_restricted(P, Sg, a, R))))
stopifnot(abs(cov_R[["restricted"]]) < 1e-12, abs(cov_R[["unrestricted"]]) > 0.1)
```

The covariance of the restricted index with the restricted trait is
`r fmt_sci(abs(cov_R[["restricted"]]))`, against `r fmt(cov_R[["unrestricted"]], 3)`
for the unrestricted index (the chunk asserts the first is below $10^{-12}$).
That is an expectation under known covariance matrices (@sec-response). What is
specific to this chapter is the object restricted and the way it is enforced: a
loss of molecular gene diversity relative to a resampling baseline, as an
inequality, by a penalty in the heuristic and as a constraint in the bound. The
rest of the lineage argument, and what it does not show, is in @sec-response.

## Relation to the standard OCS formulation

@gomezromano2016 write the general optimal-contribution problem, for a vector of
continuous contributions $\mathbf{c}$ (their eq. 1a-1d), as

$$\text{minimise} \quad \mathbf{c}'\mathbf{f}\,\mathbf{c}
  \qquad \text{subject to} \qquad
  \mathbf{c}'\mathbf{s} = 0.5,\;\; \mathbf{c}'\mathbf{d} = 0.5,\;\; c_i \ge 0,$$ {#eq-ocs-gr}

with $\mathbf{s}$ and $\mathbf{d}$ the indicators of the two sexes. The paper
writes the coancestry matrix chosen for managing diversity $\mathbf{G}$; it is
written $\mathbf{f}$ here, because $\mathbf{G}$ is the VanRaden relationship
matrix of this book (used for prediction only). The form that maximises gain
subject to a bound on $\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{c}$ is the one @sec-response
reports from the Methods of @meuwissen2020 (@meuwissen1997 reported through it
and not read for this book), up to the constant $\tfrac12$ in their group
coancestry.

@eq-ocs-problem is that constraint form restricted to
$c_i \in \{0, 1/n\}$: a fixed number $n$ of candidates contribute equally, none
partially, and the bound is set from the random-subset baseline through
@eq-ocs-theta-max. The restriction makes the problem combinatorial, which moves
the solution method from convex quadratic programming to search. It is not
arbitrary: a commercial hybrid programme plants a whole plot of a hybrid or does
not plant it.

::: {.callout-note}
## What the contributions are attached to

Three objects can carry a contribution: an individual, a line, a cross. In this
chapter $c_i$ is attached to a **hybrid**, that is, to one $A \times B$ cross
(@eq-ocs-problem), and the diversity side of that problem is optimal-contribution
selection on lines under three further restrictions (@sec-collapse). The
per-sex sum constraint of @eq-ocs-gr becomes, for hybrids of two pools, one sum
per pool. "Cross" here is the $A \times B$ hybrid. Assigning contributions to the
*within-pool* crosses that make the next generation of lines is the problem named
optimal cross selection in the title of @gorjanc2018, cited here for the name only:
that paper was not read for this book, and nothing in this chapter rests on its
content. The mating-design part (@sec-mating) does not solve that assignment: it
treats which $A \times B$ crosses to make and test under a field limit as a
sampling problem for estimation, and reviews the literature on the other in one
paragraph.
:::

## The continuous relaxation, and what it bounds {#sec-relaxation}

Drop $c_i \in \{0, 1/n\}$ to $0 \le c_i \le 1/n$ with $\sum_i c_i = 1$. For
$\lambda \ge 0$ let

$$V(\lambda) \;=\; \max_{\mathbf{c}}\; \mathbf{c}'\mathbf{u} - \lambda\,\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{c}
  \qquad \text{over} \quad \sum_i c_i = 1,\;\; 0 \le c_i \le 1/n,$$ {#eq-ocs-V}

attained at $\mathbf{c}_\lambda$, with $\bar u_\lambda = \mathbf{c}_\lambda'\mathbf{u}$
and $\theta_\lambda = \mathbf{c}_\lambda'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{c}_\lambda$, so that
$V(\lambda) = \bar u_\lambda - \lambda\,\theta_\lambda$. `ocs_relaxation()` solves it by
projected gradient, with the projection below. The cap $c_i \le 1/n$ keeps the
relaxation from putting all weight on the best candidate.

```{r}
#| label: ocs-project
project_capped_simplex
```

Two statements about $V(\lambda)$ hold and one that looks like them does not.

1. **No budget ($\lambda = 0$).** $V(0)$ is the mean of the $n$ largest $u_i$, the
   truncation plan: the relaxation is exact when there is no constraint.
2. **Weak duality.** The equal-weight vector of any set $S$ with $|S| = n$ is
   feasible in @eq-ocs-V, so for every $S$ and every $\lambda \ge 0$

   $$\bar u_S \;\le\; V(\lambda) + \lambda\,\theta_S \;=\; \bar u_\lambda + \lambda\,(\theta_S - \theta_\lambda).$$ {#eq-ocs-weak}

   Hence a relaxation point bounds every discrete plan **at least as diverse**
   as itself ($\theta_S \le \theta_\lambda$ gives $\bar u_S \le \bar u_\lambda$). For a
   plan with *less* diversity than the point, @eq-ocs-weak is the tangent of
   slope $\lambda$ at the point, which rises above the point's height.
3. **What does not follow.** A budget limits $\theta_S$ from above, and a plan
   that spends it has $\theta_S$ close to $\theta_{\max}$. For a relaxation point
   *inside* the budget ($\theta_\lambda < \theta_{\max}$) such a plan is less
   diverse than the point, and its index can exceed the point's height. The
   height of "the best relaxation point whose own $\alpha$ falls inside the
   budget" is therefore not an upper bound on the constrained problem. The book
   once used that construction; @sec-bound shows it falling below a feasible plan.

The valid statement is @eq-ocs-weak evaluated at the budget and minimised over
$\lambda$. For every $S$ with $\theta_S \le \theta_{\max}$,

$$\bar u_S \;\le\; \min_{\lambda \ge 0}\,\bigl[\,V(\lambda) + \lambda\,\theta_{\max}\bigr],$$ {#eq-ocs-bound}

and every $\lambda$ gives a valid bound, so a coarse grid of $\lambda$ costs
tightness, not validity. By Lagrangian duality for a convex programme (linear
objective, $\mathbf{f}$ positive semi-definite, Slater's condition holding when a
feasible $\mathbf{c}$ has $\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{c} < \theta_{\max}$;
@boyd2004, section 5.2.3) the minimum over *all* $\lambda$ equals the optimum of
the continuous problem $\max\,\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{u}$ with
$\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{c} \le \theta_{\max}$ in the same box, the
*continuous frontier* at the budget, and taking $\theta_{\max} = \theta_S$ in
@eq-ocs-bound shows that a discrete plan lies on or below that frontier at its
own $\alpha$. The frontier is concave in the budget, so the chord between two
points of a $\lambda$ grid lies below it, and the height of the last grid point
inside the budget is below it by an amount that depends on the grid.
`ocs_bound()` returns
the minimum over a grid (one row per $\lambda$ in @tbl-ocs-relaxation), doubles the number of projected-gradient iterations
until the bound value $V(\lambda) + \lambda\theta_{\max}$ changes by less than a relative
`tol = 1e-3`, and carries a `converged` attribute (a stalling criterion on the
doubling, not a certificate); the iteration count that converges at this scale does not
at $N = 10{,}000$ (@sec-scaling).

```{r}
#| label: ocs-relaxation-bound
# One call returns the grid of lambda, the converged relaxation points and the bound.
lam_grid <- 10^seq(0, 2.5, by = 1 / 6)           # 16 multipliers, 1 to 316
am <- 0.01                                       # the budget alpha_max
gd <- null$gd_ref
bound <- ocs_bound(ctx, n_sel, am, gd, lambdas = lam_grid)
relax <- attr(bound, "relaxation")               # one row per lambda, converged
a_relax <- (gd - relax[, "GD"]) / gd
theta_max <- 1 - gd * (1 - am)
u_top <- mean(sort(ctx$index, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(n_sel)])
stopifnot(attr(bound, "converged"),
          abs(u_top - mean_index(tr, ctx)) < 1e-12,       # V(0) = truncation
          abs(relax[1, "index"] - mean_index(tr, ctx)) < 1e-6,  # lambda = 1 already is
          isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(bound),
                           min(relax[, "index"] - relax[, "lambda"] * relax[, "theta"] +
                               relax[, "lambda"] * theta_max))))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ocs-relaxation
#| tbl-cap: "The continuous relaxation, one row per multiplier $\\lambda$ (@eq-ocs-V), from `ocs_bound()` at the 1% budget (`ocs_bound()` doubled its iterations from 4000 until the value moved by less than 0.1%). columns: $\\bar u_\\lambda$ in index s.d.; $\\theta_\\lambda$; $GD_\\lambda = 1 - \\theta_\\lambda$; $\\alpha$ of the point against `gd_ref` from `null_distribution()` ($B$ = 400 random subsets of $n$ = 60, seed 7); last column, $V(\\lambda) + \\lambda\\theta_{\\max}$ of @eq-ocs-bound at $\\alpha_{\\max}$ = 1%. Teaching scale, simulation seed 1. Four decimals."
tab_relax <- cbind(as.data.frame(relax), alpha = a_relax,
                   bound_term = relax[, "index"] - relax[, "lambda"] * relax[, "theta"] +
                                relax[, "lambda"] * theta_max)
knitr::kable(fmt(tab_relax, 4),
             col.names = c("$\\lambda$", "$\\bar u_\\lambda$", "$\\theta_\\lambda$", "$GD_\\lambda$",
                           "$\\alpha$", "$V(\\lambda) + \\lambda\\theta_{\\max}$"))
```

The first row of @tbl-ocs-relaxation coincides with the truncation plan
(statement 1; the chunk asserts it); $\alpha$ then falls as $\lambda$ rises. The last column is the quantity of
@eq-ocs-bound at each $\lambda$ of the grid; its minimum,
`r fmt(as.numeric(bound), 4)`, is at $\lambda^* =$
`r fmt(attr(bound, "lambda"), 1)`, reached with
`r attr(bound, "iters")` iterations (`converged` is
`r attr(bound, "converged")`). $\lambda^*$ is the multiplier the 1% budget
implies on this grid, in index units per unit of $\theta$; per percentage point
of $\alpha$ it is `r fmt(attr(bound, "lambda") * gd / 100, 2)` index units.

The other discrete plans are the greedy sweep over the index weight $\omega$
(argument `w` of `sel_greedy()`, score $\omega u_i - \theta$), on a logarithmic
grid of 60 values from $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-1}$. The grid is logarithmic because
the increments of $\theta$ are of order $10^{-3}$ and the differences of $u_i$ of
order 1, so $\omega$ above about $10^{-2}$ returns the truncation plan and $\omega$ below
about $10^{-5}$ returns nearly the maximum-diversity plan: the frontier lives
between.

```{r}
#| label: ocs-greedy-grid
ws <- 10^seq(-6, -1, length.out = 60)
front <- do.call(rbind, lapply(ws, function(w) {
  s <- sel_greedy(ctx, n_sel, w = w)
  data.frame(w = w, alpha = alpha_loss(s, ctx, gd), index = mean_index(s, ctx),
             Ne_par = ne_parents(s, ctx),
             theta = theta_group(s, ctx))
}))
a_trunc <- alpha_loss(tr, ctx, gd)               # alpha of the truncation plan
n_trunc <- sum(abs(front$alpha - a_trunc) < 1e-9)  # grid values that return truncation
key <- round(front[, c("alpha", "index")], 8)
n_distinct <- sum(!duplicated(key))
stopifnot(n_distinct >= 20,                      # the frontier is not degenerate
          n_trunc < nrow(front))                 # ... and it leaves truncation
inb <- front$alpha <= am
best_greedy <- max(front$index[inb])
best_relax  <- max(relax[a_relax <= am, "index"])
stopifnot(best_relax < best_greedy, best_greedy < as.numeric(bound))
```

At the 1% budget three numbers are in play. The best relaxation point of the
grid with $\alpha \le$ `r fmt(100 * am, 0)`% has index `r fmt(best_relax, 4)`; the
best greedy plan inside the budget, at $\alpha =$
`r fmt(front$alpha[inb][which.max(front$index[inb])], 5)`, has index
`r fmt(best_greedy, 4)`; the bound of @eq-ocs-bound is `r fmt(as.numeric(bound), 4)`. The chunk
asserts the order relaxation point $<$ feasible plan $<$ bound. A feasible plan
above a relaxation point inside the budget shows that the height of that point is
not a ceiling (@fig-ocs-relaxation); the bound, which is one, lies above both. The gap between the
greedy plan and the bound, `r fmt(as.numeric(bound) - best_greedy, 3)` index
units, is an upper limit on what a better search could gain at this budget on
this dataset, and only if `converged` is `TRUE`, as it is here; closing it is the
subject of @sec-advanced.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ocs-relaxation
#| fig-cap: "The continuous relaxation (grey circles, one per $\\lambda$ of @tbl-ocs-relaxation, joined by chords) and discrete plans (red: the greedy sweep of 60 index weights and three selections) on the plane of gene diversity loss $\\alpha$ against mean index. Dotted vertical line: the 1% budget. Triangle: the Lagrangian bound of @eq-ocs-bound at that budget, from `ocs_bound()` ($\\lambda$ grid of 16 values, converged). Open red circle: the best greedy plan with $\\alpha \\le$ 1%, which lies above the highest relaxation point inside the budget and below the triangle. The height of a relaxation point is not a ceiling for plans that spend more of the budget; the triangle is. Teaching scale (25 + 25 lines, 2000 markers, $n$ = 60, $N$ = 625), simulation seed 1; random: one random subset, `set.seed(42)`."
#| fig-alt: "Mean index against gene diversity loss: a grey concave curve of relaxation points, red greedy plans, and a triangle above them at the 1% budget"
set.seed(42)
sels <- list(random = sel_random(ctx, n_sel), trunc_cap = sel_truncation_cap(ctx, n_sel),
             truncation = tr)
pts <- t(sapply(sels, function(s)
  c(alpha = alpha_loss(s, ctx, gd), index = mean_index(s, ctx))))
plot(a_relax * 100, relax[, "index"], type = "b", pch = 1, lty = 2, col = book_pal[["mid"]],
     xlab = "gene diversity loss, alpha (%)", ylab = "mean index (s.d.)",
     xlim = range(c(a_relax, pts[, "alpha"], front$alpha) * 100),
     ylim = range(c(relax[, "index"], pts[, "index"], front$index, as.numeric(bound))))
points(front$alpha * 100, front$index, pch = 20, cex = 0.7, col = book_pal[["loss"]])
points(pts[, "alpha"] * 100, pts[, "index"], pch = 19, col = book_pal[["loss"]])
text(pts[, "alpha"] * 100, pts[, "index"], rownames(pts), pos = c(2, 2, 1), cex = 0.7)
j <- which(inb)[which.max(front$index[inb])]
points(front$alpha[j] * 100, front$index[j], pch = 1, cex = 1.6, col = book_pal[["loss"]])
points(am * 100, as.numeric(bound), pch = 2, cex = 1.4, lwd = 2)
abline(v = am * 100, lty = 3)
legend("bottomright",
       c("relaxation, one point per lambda", "greedy sweep and selections",
         "best greedy plan inside the budget", "Lagrangian bound at 1%"),
       col = c(book_pal[["mid"]], book_pal[["loss"]], book_pal[["loss"]], "black"), pch = c(1, 20, 1, 2),
       lty = c(2, NA, NA, NA), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
grid()
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## An under-converged relaxation reports a value that is too small

Projected gradient approaches $V(\lambda)$ from below, so an under-converged
relaxation understates $V(\lambda)$ and, with it, the bound of @eq-ocs-bound,
which then stops being one. The diagnostic is the penalised value
$V = \bar u_\lambda - \lambda\,\theta_\lambda$ (@tbl-ocs-convergence), not the index: by @eq-ocs-weak
$V(\lambda) \ge \bar u_S - \lambda\theta_S$ for every discrete plan, so a
relaxation whose $V$ is *below* a discrete plan's is not converged. The index of a converged
relaxation can lie below that of a discrete plan with no contradiction, because
the relaxation is the more diverse and pays $\lambda$ per unit of $\theta$.
:::

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ocs-convergence
#| tbl-cap: "Convergence of the relaxation at $\\lambda$ = 10 against the number of projected-gradient iterations. columns: $\\bar u_\\lambda$; $\\theta_\\lambda$; $V = \\bar u_\\lambda - \\lambda\\theta_\\lambda$, the penalised value. Last row: the truncation plan, which is discrete (V computed with its own index and $\\theta$). Teaching scale, simulation seed 1; four decimals."
lam <- 10
its <- c(50, 500, 4000, 16000)
conv <- do.call(rbind, lapply(its, function(it) {
  r <- ocs_relaxation(ctx, n_sel, lam, iters = it)
  data.frame(iterations = it, index = r[, "index"], theta = r[, "theta"],
             V = r[, "index"] - lam * r[, "theta"], row.names = NULL)
}))
disc <- data.frame(iterations = NA, index = mean_index(tr, ctx),
                   theta = theta_group(tr, ctx),
                   V = mean_index(tr, ctx) - lam * theta_group(tr, ctx))
rel_change <- abs(conv$V[4] - conv$V[3]) / abs(conv$V[3])
stopifnot(conv$V[1] < disc$V,                # 50 iterations: V below a feasible plan
          conv$V[3] >= disc$V,               # 4000 iterations: V above it
          all(diff(conv$V) >= 0),            # V rises with iterations
          rel_change < 1e-3)                 # the tol of ocs_bound(), applied here to V
# weak duality (eq. ocs-weak) for every discrete plan of the chapter, lambda = 10
plans <- c(sels, lapply(seq_len(nrow(front)), function(i) sel_greedy(ctx, n_sel, w = front$w[i])))
Vplan <- vapply(plans, function(s) mean_index(s, ctx) - lam * theta_group(s, ctx), numeric(1))
stopifnot(all(Vplan <= conv$V[4] + 1e-8))
knitr::kable(fmt(rbind(conv, disc), 4),
             col.names = c("iterations", "$\\bar u_\\lambda$", "$\\theta_\\lambda$",
                           "$V = \\bar u_\\lambda - \\lambda\\theta_\\lambda$"))
```

At 50 iterations $V$ is `r fmt(conv$V[1], 4)`, below the discrete plan's
`r fmt(disc$V, 4)`; at 4000 it is `r fmt(conv$V[3], 4)`, above; from 4000 to
16000 it moves by `r fmt_sci(100 * rel_change)`% (@tbl-ocs-convergence). The chunk
asserts that ordering, that $V$ does not fall as iterations grow, that the relative change
in $V$ from 4000 to 16000 iterations is below $10^{-3}$, and that no discrete plan of the chapter (all
`r length(plans)` of them) has a penalised value above the converged $V$. The
tolerance is the same relative $10^{-3}$ as the `tol` of `ocs_bound()`, but
`ocs_bound()` applies it to the bound value $V(\lambda) + \lambda\theta_{\max}$,
not to $V$ at $\lambda = 10$. "Converged" here means that relative change at
$\lambda = 10$ at this scale: a stalling criterion, the value stopped moving as
the count grew, not a certificate that it equals $V(\lambda)$. This chapter does not
measure larger $\lambda$ or larger $N$; `ocs_bound()` doubles the count and
checks the change in the bound value at each $\lambda$ grid it is given, rather
than assuming that a count that stalls here stalls there.

## Setting the budget

The budget should not be chosen a priori. Pure truncation, the unconstrained
optimum of the index, has loss $\alpha_{\text{trunc}}$: the $\alpha$ at which the
constraint stops binding. It is not the largest $\alpha$ any $n$-subset reaches
(a minimum-diversity selection would exceed it); it is the largest a
gain-maximising selection ever needs (@sec-baseline). A budget
$\alpha_{\max} \ge \alpha_{\text{trunc}}$ restricts nothing, and
`stage2_select()` warns about any requested $\alpha$ above this ceiling rather
than return an unconstrained plan that looks constrained. Here
$\alpha_{\text{trunc}} =$ `r fmt(a_trunc, 4)` for $B$ = 400 random subsets; it
depends on $B$ in the third decimal.

@fig-ocs-frontier traces what each budget costs: the greedy frontier over the
index weight $\omega$ of the grid above. The frontier is the set of
feasible plans the greedy finds; it is a lower bound on the constrained optimum,
not the optimum. @tbl-ocs-frontier lists a subset of its plans.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ocs-frontier
#| fig-alt: "Mean index against gene diversity loss for the distinct greedy plans, rising and flattening towards the truncation plan"
#| fig-cap: "The greedy frontier over the index weight $\\omega$ (60 values, logarithmic from $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-1}$): mean index against gene diversity loss $\\alpha$, one point per distinct plan; plans that coincide are drawn once. Dashed red line: $\\alpha_{\\text{trunc}}$, the loss of the truncation plan; dotted: the 1% budget of @fig-ocs-relaxation. Teaching scale, simulation seed 1, $n$ = 60, $N$ = 625; $\\alpha$ against `gd_ref` from $B$ = 400 random subsets (seed 7)."
fd <- front[!duplicated(key), ]
fd <- fd[order(fd$alpha), ]
plot(fd$alpha * 100, fd$index, type = "b", pch = 19, col = book_pal[["ink"]],
     xlab = "gene diversity loss, alpha (%)", ylab = "mean index (s.d.)")
abline(v = a_trunc * 100, lty = 2, col = book_pal[["loss"]])
abline(v = am * 100, lty = 3)
text(a_trunc * 100, min(fd$index), "truncation", pos = 2, cex = 0.7, col = book_pal[["loss"]])
grid()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ocs-frontier
#| tbl-cap: "Every sixth distinct plan of the greedy frontier of @fig-ocs-frontier, in order of $\\alpha$. columns: index weight $\\omega$; $\\alpha$ (proportion); mean index $\\bar u_S$ (s.d.); effective number of parents $N_{e,\\text{par}}$. Four decimals; teaching scale, simulation seed 1."
sub <- fd[seq(1, nrow(fd), by = 6), c("w", "alpha", "index", "Ne_par")]
sub$w <- format(sub$w, digits = 2, scientific = TRUE)    # w spans five decades
knitr::kable(fmt(sub, 4), row.names = FALSE, col.names = c("$\\omega$", "$\\alpha$", "$\\bar u_S$", "$N_{e,\\text{par}}$"))
# secant slopes of the frontier between fixed levels of alpha (percent)
lev <- c(-1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 100 * a_trunc)
ip <- approx(fd$alpha * 100, fd$index, xout = lev)$y
secant <- diff(ip) / diff(lev)               # index per percentage point of alpha
```

Of the 60 values of $\omega$, `r n_distinct` give distinct plans and
`r n_trunc` return the truncation plan (@tbl-ocs-frontier). Linear interpolation of the distinct plans gives, between
$\alpha$ = -1, 0, 1, 2, 3% and $\alpha_{\text{trunc}}$, a secant slope of
`r paste(fmt(secant, 2), collapse = ", ")` index units per percentage point of
$\alpha$. This shows that on this dataset the cost of diversity is largest at low $\alpha$ and
falls towards $\alpha_{\text{trunc}}$; the greedy frontier is a heuristic, not
the optimum, and the slopes are secants of a noisy curve. It does not locate a sharp knee, and none is
claimed. Where along it to set the budget is the committee's decision. A grid of $\omega$
in the wrong units (the integers $1, 2, 3, \dots$, say) returns the truncation
plan for every value and the frontier collapses to one point; the grid has to be in the units of $\omega$
that move the plan, which is why the chunk asserts that the sweep has at least
20 distinct plans.

### How $\alpha_{\text{trunc}}$ moves when $\mathbf{f}$ moves

$\alpha_{\text{trunc}}$ is quoted to four decimals, which invites more
confidence than the marker panel supports. The same panel feeds $\mathbf{f}$ and
therefore $GD_{\text{ref}}$ and $\alpha_{\text{trunc}}$. In the experiment below
$\mathbf{f}$, the null and $\alpha_{\text{trunc}}$ are rebuilt under a minor-allele-frequency
(MAF) filter, a density and an ascertainment scenario (@tbl-ocs-panel-seed1), **but the index is not**:
`ctx$traits` stays the one made from all markers, so A5 (the panel is the causal
set) is dropped here and the result concerns a fixed index with a thinned
$\mathbf{f}$, not a change of genotyping platform. Each panel's null is
`null_distribution()` with its default seed 7, so the random subsets are the
same draws of hybrids in every panel.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ocs-panel-seed1
#| tbl-cap: "$GD_{\\text{ref}}$ and $\\alpha_{\\text{trunc}}$ under five marker panels, one founder draw (simulation seed 1, teaching scale, $n$ = 60). markers: panel size; $GD_{\\text{ref}}$: mean $GD$ of $B$ = 250 random subsets; $\\alpha_{\\text{trunc}}$: loss of the truncation plan. MAF filters on the frozen pool frequencies `ctx$p0`; the last row keeps the markers polymorphic in pool A. Four decimals."
ceiling_for <- function(keep, label, B = 250) {
  Xs <- ctx$X[, keep, drop = FALSE]
  ck <- build_ctx(X = Xs, f = molecular_coancestry(Xs), G = NULL,
                  traits = ctx$traits, ped = ctx$ped, n_lines = ctx$n_lines,
                  pool = ctx$pool, fL = NULL, cfg = ctx$cfg)
  nl <- null_distribution(ck, n_sel, B = B, B_full = 1)
  data.frame(panel = label, markers = ncol(Xs), gd_ref = nl$gd_ref,
             alpha_trunc = alpha_loss(sel_truncation(ck, n_sel), ck, nl$gd_ref))
}
maf <- pmin(ctx$p0, 1 - ctx$p0)
polyA <- colMeans(simulate_lines(book_cfg)[seq_len(book_cfg$n_pool_A), ] / 2)
sens <- rbind(
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.10),
    function(t) ceiling_for(maf >= t, sprintf("MAF >= %.2f", t)))),
  ceiling_for(polyA > 0 & polyA < 1, "ascertained in pool A"))
knitr::kable(fmt(sens, 4),
             col.names = c("panel", "markers", "$GD_{\\text{ref}}$", "$\\alpha_{\\text{trunc}}$"))
```

On this founder draw $GD_{\text{ref}}$ moves by
`r fmt(100 * (max(sens$gd_ref) / min(sens$gd_ref) - 1), 0)`% across these
panels and $\alpha_{\text{trunc}}$ by
`r fmt(100 * (max(sens$alpha_trunc) / min(sens$alpha_trunc) - 1), 1)`%
(@tbl-ocs-panel-seed1). One founder draw does not say how typical that is. The
same five panels, with the thinning of @tbl-ocs-thin, were rebuilt on 20 founder draws
(simulation seeds 1 to 20; @tbl-ocs-panel-spread; `Rscript book/scripts/regenerate.R ocs_panel`, which
writes `book/data/ocs_panel_sweep.csv` and is reproducible from this
repository).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ocs-panel-spread
#| tbl-cap: "Movement of $GD_{\\text{ref}}$ and of $\\alpha_{\\text{trunc}}$ across the five marker panels of @tbl-ocs-panel-seed1, over 20 founder draws (simulation seeds 1 to 20; teaching scale, $n$ = 60). For each draw the movement is $100(\\max/\\min - 1)$ over the five panels, in percent. Rows: mean, s.d., minimum, maximum and median over the 20 draws, and the value of seed 1. Two decimals."
sw <- read.csv(book_data("ocs_panel_sweep.csv"))
five <- sw[!grepl("thinned", sw[["panel"]]), ]
mv <- function(v) tapply(v, five[["seed"]], function(x) 100 * (max(x) / min(x) - 1))
m_gd <- mv(five[["gd_ref"]]); m_al <- mv(five[["alpha_trunc"]])
stopifnot(length(m_al) == 20, isTRUE(all.equal(unname(m_al[1]),
  100 * (max(sens$alpha_trunc) / min(sens$alpha_trunc) - 1), tolerance = 1e-6)))
sm <- function(x) c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x), min = min(x), max = max(x),
                    median = median(x), seed1 = x[[1]])
knitr::kable(fmt(data.frame(statistic = names(sm(m_gd)), gd_ref = sm(m_gd),
                            alpha_trunc = sm(m_al), row.names = NULL), 2),
             col.names = c("statistic", "$GD_{\\text{ref}}$ movement (%)",
                           "$\\alpha_{\\text{trunc}}$ movement (%)"))
```

Across the 20 draws $GD_{\text{ref}}$ moves by a mean of
`r fmt(mean(m_gd), 1)`% (range `r fmt(min(m_gd), 1)` to `r fmt(max(m_gd), 1)`%) and
$\alpha_{\text{trunc}}$ by a mean of `r fmt(mean(m_al), 1)`% (s.d.
`r fmt(sd(m_al), 1)`, range `r fmt(min(m_al), 1)` to `r fmt(max(m_al), 1)`%), about
`r fmt(mean(m_gd) / mean(m_al), 1)` times less than the level; seed 1, the
draw of @tbl-ocs-panel-seed1, is `r fmt(m_al[[1]], 1)`%, below the median of
`r fmt(median(m_al), 1)`%. The chunk asserts that the seed-1 value of this file equals
the live value of @tbl-ocs-panel-seed1. This measures that the budget
ceiling moves less than the diversity level it is computed from, not that it
does not move. A ratio of two diversities measured on the same panel cancels the
part of the shift that numerator and denominator share; the table shows that
cancellation is partial. A budget is therefore more portable across panels than
$GD_{\text{ref}}$, not invariant to them, and the spread is a property of this
simulator at this scale (25 + 25 lines, 2000 markers), not measured at another.

Density adds noise (@tbl-ocs-thin). Each draw's panel was thinned to 250, 500 and 1000 markers,
six independent subsets each, the subsets drawn before any `null_distribution()` call
(the callout on `null_distribution()` below).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ocs-thin
#| tbl-cap: "$\\alpha_{\\text{trunc}}$ under random thinning of the marker panel, over 20 founder draws (simulation seeds 1 to 20; teaching scale, $n$ = 60). The full-panel value is from $B$ = 250 random subsets, the thinned values from $B$ = 200. markers: panel size (full panel 2000); bias: mean over draws of (mean of 6 thinned subsets minus the full-panel $\\alpha_{\\text{trunc}}$); s.e. of bias: its standard error over draws; rel. s.d.: s.d. of the 6 subsets divided by their mean, in percent, median, minimum and maximum over draws; draws within 1 s.d.: draws, of 20, in which the mean of the 6 subsets lies within one s.d. of the full-panel value. Four decimals for the bias, one for rel_sd."
full <- sw[sw[["panel"]] == "MAF >= 0.00", c("seed", "alpha_trunc")]
names(full)[2] <- "a_full"
th <- merge(sw[grepl("thinned", sw[["panel"]]), ], full, by = "seed")
agg <- function(d) {
  m <- mean(d$alpha_trunc); s <- sd(d$alpha_trunc)
  data.frame(m = m, s = s, diff = m - d$a_full[1])
}
by_draw <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(th, list(th$markers, th$seed)), function(d)
  cbind(markers = d$markers[1], seed = d$seed[1], agg(d))))
stopifnot(nrow(by_draw) == 60)
thin_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(by_draw, by_draw$markers), function(d)
  data.frame(markers = d$markers[1], bias = mean(d$diff),
             se = sd(d$diff) / sqrt(nrow(d)),
             rel_sd_median = median(100 * d$s / d$m),
             rel_sd_min = min(100 * d$s / d$m), rel_sd_max = max(100 * d$s / d$m),
             within_1sd = sum(abs(d$diff) <= d$s))))
thin_tab[c("bias", "se")] <- lapply(thin_tab[c("bias", "se")], formatC, format = "f", digits = 4)
knitr::kable(fmt(thin_tab, 1), row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("markers", "bias", "s.e. of bias", "rel. s.d. median (%)",
                           "rel. s.d. min (%)", "rel. s.d. max (%)", "draws within 1 s.d."))
```

At 250 markers the mean over six subsets differs from the full-panel value by
`r thin_tab$bias[thin_tab$markers == 250]` on average
(s.e. `r thin_tab$se[thin_tab$markers == 250]` over draws), inside one
s.d. of the six subsets in `r thin_tab$within_1sd[thin_tab$markers == 250]` of 20
draws; the s.d. itself is a median of
`r fmt(thin_tab$rel_sd_median[thin_tab$markers == 250], 0)`% of the estimate
(range `r fmt(thin_tab$rel_sd_min[thin_tab$markers == 250], 0)` to
`r fmt(thin_tab$rel_sd_max[thin_tab$markers == 250], 0)`%) (@tbl-ocs-thin). That is a
measurement on six subsets per cell, with no interval on the s.d. itself. What
it supports is that no bias of a thin panel's $\alpha_{\text{trunc}}$ was detected
over founder draws, at a resolution of about
`r fmt(2 * as.numeric(thin_tab$se[thin_tab$markers == 250]), 3)` (two standard
errors at 250 markers, against a mean full-panel $\alpha_{\text{trunc}}$ of
`r fmt(mean(full$a_full), 3)`), so a bias of a few percent of $\alpha_{\text{trunc}}$ is
not excluded; and that a single study gets an estimate with a relative spread of a
third. A single thin-panel study cannot tell which side of the full-panel value
it landed on.

:::: {.callout-warning}
## `null_distribution()` reseeds, and will freeze a resampling loop

It calls `set.seed(seed)` on entry, with `seed = 7` by default, so the random
stream is reset every time it is invoked. Any `sample()` written *after* it
inside a loop draws the same values on every pass, and a replication study
becomes one replicate reported with a spurious standard deviation. The chunk
checks the mechanism.

```{r}
#| label: ocs-reseed
draw_after_null <- function() {
  null_distribution(ctx, n_sel, B = 5, B_full = 1)
  sample.int(ctx$m, 5)
}
stopifnot(identical(draw_after_null(), draw_after_null()))
```

Draw randomisation up front, as the cached sweep does, or pass a varying `seed`.
::::

:::: {.callout-warning}
## Quote $\alpha_{\text{trunc}}$ and the budget with the panel that produced them

$\alpha_{\text{trunc}}$ is a property of the germplasm *and* the marker panel.
Re-derive it whenever the panel changes and do not compare an $\alpha$ across
studies genotyped differently. The spread measured above is across founder draws
at one platform and one scale; it is not a measure of the difference between two
real platforms.
::::

## A caveat carried over from the OCS literature

@gomezromano2016 (p. 7, their Fig. 1 and p. 8, their Fig. 2) study contributions
optimised under a restriction on the rate of *regional* genomic coancestry (the
whole genome except one chromosome, strategy CHR_ove), with populations of
$N = 20, 100, 200$ candidates. They compute the expected rate of coancestry in
the next generation as follows (@eq-ocs-gr-delta):

$$E(\Delta f_{t+1}) \;=\; \frac{\mathbf{c}_t'\,\mathbf{G}_{x,t}\,\mathbf{c}_t - f_t}{1 - f_t},$$ {#eq-ocs-gr-delta}

with $\mathbf{c}_t$ the contributions, $\mathbf{G}_{x,t}$ the coancestry matrix of
the candidates computed from marker genotypes (for the region in question) and $f_t$
the mean coancestry of the candidates' generation (written $\mathbf{f}$ and $\bar f$
elsewhere in this book). Two measurements are reported.

- Fig. 1: with the restriction set at 0.1%, the realised rate was approximately
  1.4%, 0.3% and 0.2% for $N = 20, 100, 200$, always above the restriction while
  the expected rate met it; the gap between expected and realised rate tended
  to grow as $N$ fell.
- Fig. 2: for three sets of parents with the contributions held fixed, 1000
  offspring generations were drawn; the realised average coancestry was always
  above the expected value, and the observed rate was approximately double the
  intended rate (at $N = 20$).

The paper's Discussion (p. 11) states that the predicted value "was consistently
biased downward" and that the bias grew as $N$ fell, and suggests that terms from
Mendelian inheritance variance are missing from an equation derived for the
infinitesimal model with pedigree coancestry; that is the authors' suggestion,
not a derivation. No single factor of two follows from these: it is about 2 in
one resampling analysis at $N = 20$ and about 14, 3 and 2 against the restriction
at $N = 20, 100, 200$. Whether the same bias holds for the whole-genome
$\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{c}$ of this book, at other $N$ and for hybrids, is
not shown by that paper.

This does **not** affect the $\theta_S$ computed in this book: $\mathbf{f}$ is
measured on the marker genotypes of an already-realised hybrid population, with no
forward-prediction step. It becomes relevant when the pipeline plans a further
generation from the selected hybrids, predicting *their* offspring's coancestry
from a contribution vector: the direction of the bias reported is that
$\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{f}\mathbf{c}$ underestimates the realised coancestry, and a
budget on a predicted coancestry would need a margin whose size is not measured here.

## Quadratic programming, when contributions are continuous

Where the problem genuinely is continuous (composing a synthetic, assembling a core
collection, setting seed proportions) it is solved as a quadratic programme (QP) rather
than by search: `optimal_contributions()` of @sec-subdivided, with
`ocs_quadprog()` adding the merit term. The example below (@tbl-ocs-qp) uses all 50 lines, with
$\mathbf{f}^L$ the line coancestry and, as the merit of a line, **the mean index of
the hybrids that use it as a parent** (`line_merit`). That is a value of the line
against a tester, the other pool as a whole (not the line alone), computed on the
known index and not on a prediction. `quadprog` is a `Suggests` package; the chunk runs only
where it is installed.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ocs-qp
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("quadprog", quietly = TRUE)
#| tbl-cap: "Continuous optimal contributions on the 50 lines of the teaching scale (`ocs_quadprog()`), one row per penalty $\\lambda$, with each line capped at 20% of the pooled contribution (`upper` = 0.20). merit: $\\mathbf{c}'\\mathbf{g}$ with $g_a$ the mean index of the hybrids that have line $a$ as a parent; coancestry: $\\mathbf{c}'\\mathbf{f}^L\\mathbf{c}$; lines used: lines with $c_a > 10^{-6}$; share of pool A: total contribution of pool A. Four decimals."
pa <- as.integer(ctx$ped$a); pb <- as.integer(ctx$ped$b)
line_merit <- vapply(seq_len(ctx$n_lines),
                     function(a) mean(ctx$index[pa == a | pb == a]), numeric(1))
front_qp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(10^seq(-1, 2, length.out = 8), function(lam) {
  o <- ocs_quadprog(ctx$fL, line_merit, lambda = lam, upper = 0.20)
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(sum(o$c_i), 1, tolerance = 1e-4)),
            all(o$c_i <= 0.20 + 1e-5))
  data.frame(lambda = lam, merit = o$merit, coancestry = o$coancestry,
             n_used = sum(o$c_i > 1e-6), share_A = sum(o$c_i[ctx$pool == "A"]))
}))
knitr::kable(fmt(front_qp, 4),
             col.names = c("$\\lambda$", "merit", "coancestry", "lines used", "share of pool A"))
```

`upper = 0.20` is a share of the pooled contribution, which sums to one over the 50
lines, with a single margin: the QP of @sec-subdivided has no per-pool sum, and
the share of pool A shows what that permits (the hybrid problem requires each pool to
carry one half; @sec-collapse). The cap `max_use` of the discrete problem is a count of hybrids;
in contribution weights $w_a = k_a/(2n)$ (with $k_a$ the number of times line $a$ is a
parent of the $n$ selected hybrids, so $\sum_a w_a = 1$) it is $w_a \le \texttt{max\_use}/(2n)$, so `upper`
$= \texttt{max\_use}/(2n)$ puts the two on one scale, and `upper = 0.20` at $n$ = 60
corresponds to `max_use` = `r 0.20 * 2 * n_sel`. They are the same restriction in kind, an
operational ceiling on one line's use that is easier to defend than the $\lambda$
that produced it, not the same constraint: the first caps a share of a
continuous vector, the second a count in a discrete selection enforced in the
decoder (@sec-combinatorial). The chunk asserts that each solution sums to one and
respects the cap.

As $\lambda$ falls the solution concentrates on fewer lines, which the lines-used column
shows, down to the five lines that the 20% cap allows at least. The same mechanism makes $N_{e,\text{par}}$ a second restriction in the
discrete problem of @sec-choosing-recommendation; the fitness printed above
carries only the budget (and, when set, `max_use`), not $N_{e,\text{par}}$. The merit here has no
correlated prediction error, so the concentration shown is the concentration of
the truth; the effect of selecting on predicted values, where error is correlated
with relatedness, is @sec-choosing-error.

## What belongs in the inner loop

The optimiser performs on the order of $10^5$ to $10^6$ evaluations (the defaults of
`sel_de()` give `NP` x `itermax` =
`r format(prod(unlist(formals(sel_de)[c("NP", "itermax")])), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)`
fitness calls at most), so the cost per call decides what goes into the objective
and what waits for validation. @sec-choosing-cost times the metrics and reports
that the matrix route and the line route of @sec-collapse agree to numerical
precision, that the line route is slower per call at $N = 2{,}500$, $n = 50$ and
cheaper only for large $n$, and that it is the only one that exists at
$N = 22{,}500$: it is the route that scales, not a faster call at the scale of
this chapter. This chapter
times nothing. What @sec-choosing-recommendation puts in the objective is $\theta$
(by the matrix or line route) and $N_{e,\text{par}}$; allelic richness and A-NE (accession-to-nearest-entry distance, @sec-catalogue) are
kept for validation of the returned plan. This chapter computes none of them,
nor Nei's $G_{st}$ (`gst()`); where they are computed, and at what cost, is
@sec-choosing-cost and @sec-choosing-recommendation.

<!-- reproduce-chapter -->

## Reproduce this chapter {.unnumbered}

All the code of this chapter, in order and with the explanation kept as comments, is one script: [**09-optimal-contributions.R**](https://ederdbs.github.io/QG/downloads/09-optimal-contributions.R){download="09-optimal-contributions.R"}.
Download it, install `hybdiv`, and run it top to bottom in an empty directory; cached results are fetched on first use.
